title: Progressive Web Apps Practice
description: Practise the twelve ideas in this Progressive Web Apps course. Choose an answer, then read why it fits the example.

exercises.question: What should work before PWA extras are added?
options: The normal website
Only a push notification service
exercises.explanation: A progressive web app starts as a working website. Extra features should help even when installation or offline support is not available.

exercises.question: What kind of file is this manifest?
options: A database of passwords
A JSON description of the web app
exercises.explanation: A manifest is a JSON file that describes the app name, start address and display choices. A browser can use it when offering installation.

exercises.question: How does the page point to its manifest?
options: A link with rel="manifest"
An h1 containing the file name
exercises.explanation: The page must link its manifest. Icons should be real image files in the sizes declared by the manifest.

exercises.question: Why check "serviceWorker" in navigator?
options: To create a new user account
To see whether this browser supports the feature
exercises.explanation: A service worker is a script that the browser can run separately from the page. It can handle requests within its scope.

exercises.question: Why call event.waitUntil?
options: To let the browser wait for the cache job
To pause the browser forever
exercises.explanation: The install event is a chance to prepare files for later use. waitUntil keeps the install job open while those files are saved.

exercises.question: When is the offline fallback used here?
options: For every successful network request
When a navigation network request fails
exercises.explanation: A fetch handler can try the network first and use a saved page when that request fails. Limit the rule to the kind of request you intend to handle.

exercises.question: Why clone the response before caching it?
options: The cache and caller each need a readable response body
Cloning changes the file colour
exercises.explanation: Cache-first uses a stored response before trying the network. It suits files whose addresses change when their contents change.

exercises.question: Why use a reading- prefix check?
options: To delete all browser history
To avoid deleting caches owned by another app
exercises.explanation: The activate event can tidy old cache versions. Use a clear prefix so your worker only removes caches it owns.

exercises.question: Why can an installed worker be waiting?
options: An older version still controls open pages
Its file must be named wait.js
exercises.explanation: A new worker may wait while the old one still controls open pages. This avoids mixing a new app version with an old page halfway through a task.

exercises.question: Where is this choice stored?
options: Automatically on every device
In this browser for this site
exercises.explanation: A page can remember a small choice in localStorage. This storage belongs to that browser and origin, not to a cloud account.

exercises.question: Does an online event guarantee that a server can be reached?
options: No, the actual request can still fail
Yes, every server must be available
exercises.explanation: The online and offline events are useful clues. A device can report online even when a particular server cannot be reached.

exercises.question: Why test a first visit separately from a repeat visit?
options: Repeat visits never use a network
The first visit may have no saved files yet
exercises.explanation: A PWA needs tests for first visit, repeat visit, offline use and updates. Old workers and caches can hide mistakes during development.
